title: Pick the plain step
prompt: Which instruction would a tired mechanic get right the first time?

options.text: It is recommended that the valve be closed prior to removal of the pump.
options.why: Passive, long, and "prior to" / "recommended" hide what to do.

options.text: Close the valve. Then remove the pump.
options.why: One action per sentence, active voice, simple words.

options.text: Closing of the valve should ideally happen before pump removal.
options.why: "Should ideally" makes it optional, and no one is told to act.

title: Spot the fancy words
prompt: Tap the 2 words a Simplified English writer would replace.
sentence: Utilize the torque wrench prior to installing the cover.
explain: "Utilize" → "use", "prior to" → "before". Short, common words have one meaning.

title: Simple words only
prompt: Which explains a "cloud backup" to your grandmother?

options.text: Your files are replicated to redundant off-site storage infrastructure.
options.why: Every second word needs a dictionary.

options.text: A copy of your photos is kept on another computer far away, so you won't lose them.
options.why: Everyday words, and it says why it matters.

options.text: It's like the cloud, but for backups.
options.why: Explains the word with itself. Nothing learned.

title: Too technical
prompt: Tap the 3 words that aren't everyday words.
sentence: The application authenticates your credentials before you can see your account.
explain: Try: "The app checks your name and password before you can see your account."

title: Bottom line first
prompt: Your manager will read only the first line. Which one should it be?

options.text: Hope you had a good weekend! Quick update on the vendor thing from last week.
options.why: Friendly, but the reader still doesn't know what you need.

options.text: As you know, the vendor sent new pricing, and there are a few things to consider.
options.why: Background first. The point is still hidden.

options.text: Please approve the 18% vendor price rise by Friday, or the rollout slips to Q4.
options.why: The decision, the deadline and the cost, all in line one.

title: Lead with the ask
prompt: Which subject line gets the right action fastest?

options.text: Server stuff
options.why: Says nothing about what's needed or when.

options.text: Action by 5pm: approve downtime for Saturday 2am patch
options.why: Action, deadline and topic. Readers can triage it in a second.

options.text: Some thoughts about the upcoming maintenance window
options.why: Sounds optional, and the ask is buried.

title: Find the fog
prompt: Tap the 2 vague words a customer could argue about.
sentence: We reply to most urgent tickets soon.
explain: "Most" — which ones? "Soon" — within what time? Replace each with a number.

title: Can you check it?
prompt: Which promise could a customer and a manager both check?

options.text: We aim to respond quickly to important issues.
options.why: "Quickly" and "important" mean different things to different people.

options.text: We reply to every P1 ticket within 1 hour, 24/7.
options.why: A defined class, a number and the hours. Anyone can verify it.

options.text: We reply as soon as reasonably possible.
options.why: Always true, so it promises nothing.

title: And, or, or both?
prompt: "Members get free shipping and/or a 5% discount." Can a member get both?

options.text: Yes
options.why: Maybe — but another reader will say no.

options.text: No
options.why: Maybe — but another reader will say yes.

options.text: The sentence doesn't say
options.why: "And/or" lets the reader pick. Write "free shipping, a 5% discount, or both".

title: Who is "she"?
prompt: "The manager told the engineer that she was promoted." Who was promoted?

options.text: The manager
options.why: Possible — but so is the engineer.

options.text: The engineer
options.why: Possible — but so is the manager.

options.text: You can't tell
options.why: "She" can point to either person. Repeat the noun: "…that the engineer was promoted".

title: Pointing at what?
prompt: Tap every word that could point to two different things.
sentence: When the app sends the file to the server, it compresses it.
explain: Does the app compress the file, or does the server compress something? Name the actor and the object.

title: Spot the EARS shape
prompt: Which sentence follows an EARS template?

options.text: The door locks itself after a while.
options.why: No trigger, no "shall", and "a while" is vague.

options.text: When the door has been closed for 30 seconds, the controller shall lock the door.
options.why: When <trigger>, the <system> shall <response>. Testable.

options.text: Locking should happen automatically if needed.
options.why: Who locks? When is it "needed"? "Should" is a wish.

title: Wish or rule?
prompt: Tap the word that turns this requirement into a wish.
sentence: When the battery falls below 20%, the drone should return to the launch point.

title: What's the claim?
prompt: What is the writer's main claim?
source: Our onboarding has seven screens. Half of new users quit before the last one. Teams that cut onboarding to two screens doubled activation. We should cut ours to two.

options.text: Half of new users quit onboarding.
options.why: That's evidence, not the claim.

options.text: We should cut onboarding to two screens.
options.why: That's what the writer wants us to accept and act on.

options.text: Other teams doubled activation.
options.why: Another piece of evidence for the claim.

title: Reason or claim?
prompt: "We should move the standup to 10am because half the team starts at 9:30." Which part is the reason?

options.text: We should move the standup to 10am
options.why: That's the claim — what we're asked to do.

options.text: half the team starts at 9:30
options.why: It's offered as support for the claim.

options.text: Neither — it's just an opinion
options.why: It has a clear claim and a reason; whether the reason is good is another question.

title: The missing link
prompt: "Sales rose after we changed the logo, so the new logo works." What does this quietly assume?

options.text: That nothing else that month (season, prices, ads) caused the rise.
options.why: After ≠ because. The argument needs the logo to be the cause.

options.text: That the old logo was blue.
options.why: Irrelevant to whether the conclusion follows.

options.text: That sales are measured in dollars.
options.why: The unit doesn't matter here.

title: Correlation trap
prompt: "People who use our premium plan churn less, so upselling everyone to premium will cut churn." What's the weak spot?

options.text: Premium is more expensive.
options.why: True, but not why the reasoning fails.

options.text: Loyal customers may choose premium — premium may not create loyalty.
options.why: The cause might run the other way (or a third factor drives both).

options.text: Churn is hard to spell.
options.why: Nice try.

title: Find the steelman
prompt: You support remote work. Which is the strongest fair version of the other side?

options.text: People just want to slack off at home.
options.why: That's a strawman: weak and unfair.

options.text: New hires learn much faster by overhearing and asking in person, and that mentoring is hard to rebuild remotely.
options.why: Specific, plausible, and something a real opponent would say.

options.text: Offices are nice.
options.why: True, maybe, but not an argument.

title: Spot the strawman
prompt: Someone says: "We should add tests before refactoring." Which reply attacks a strawman?

options.text: Tests take time; for this one-line change the risk seems low.
options.why: Engages with the actual proposal.

options.text: So you want us to stop shipping until we reach 100% coverage?
options.why: It swaps their claim for an extreme one that's easy to knock down.

options.text: Which parts are riskiest? Let's test those first.
options.why: A constructive, fair response.

title: Who's missing?
prompt: "All the users we interviewed love the new design." Who might be missing from this picture?

options.text: Users who left because of the new design
options.why: If you only ask people who stayed, you only hear from people who like it (survivorship bias).

options.text: The designers
options.why: They're not the users being described.

options.text: Nobody — interviews are always representative
options.why: Interview groups are rarely a fair sample.

title: Loaded words
prompt: Tap the 2 words that slip in an unproven assumption.
sentence: Obviously everyone prefers dark mode, so make it the default.
explain: "Obviously" skips the evidence; "everyone" claims a 100% that nobody measured.

title: Can't build that
prompt: Tap the word a developer can't implement as written.
explain: 15 minutes? 24 hours? Two developers will pick two numbers.

title: The unasked question
prompt: "A user can request a reset link by email." Which question does this spec NOT answer?

options.text: Does a newer link cancel the older ones?
options.why: Request twice, and two teams will build two different behaviours.

options.text: How does the user ask for a link?
options.why: The spec says: by email.

options.text: Who can request a link?
options.why: The spec says: a user.

title: Which 30 days?
prompt: Which refund rule leaves no room for two agents to disagree?

options.text: Refunds within 30 days.
options.why: 30 days from what? Purchase, shipping or delivery?

options.text: Refunds within 30 calendar days of the delivery date shown in tracking.
options.why: Start point, day type and source of truth are all fixed.

options.text: Refunds within about a month.
options.why: "About" invites arguments.

title: Agents will argue
prompt: Tap the 2 words two support agents could read differently.
sentence: Items must be returned in good condition within a reasonable time.
explain: "Good condition" — box opened? tags missing? "Reasonable time" — whose idea of reasonable?

title: Whose hours?
prompt: Ana is in London and Ben in San Francisco. "Book the first free hour during working hours." What's undefined?

options.text: Whose working hours count
options.why: London 9–5 and San Francisco 9–5 barely overlap. The spec doesn't say which applies.

options.text: How long the meeting is
options.why: The spec says one hour.

options.text: Who should attend
options.why: Ana and Ben.

title: When nothing fits
prompt: Everyone's calendar is full next week. What does "book the first free slot next week" do?

options.text: Books the week after
options.why: The spec never says that.

options.text: Shows an error
options.why: The spec never says that either.

options.text: Undefined — the spec forgot the empty case
options.why: Always ask: what happens when the answer is "nothing"?

title: Always true
prompt: Which of these is an invariant — true in every state, not just at the end?

options.text: After a transfer, an email is sent.
options.why: That's an event that happens once, not a rule for every state.

options.text: The sum of the two balances never changes during a transfer.
options.why: True before, during and after — even if the server crashes midway.

options.text: Transfers should be fast.
options.why: A wish, and vague.

title: Never, ever
prompt: Which state must an elevator NEVER be in?

options.text: Doors open, car stopped at a floor
options.why: That's how people get in and out.

options.text: Doors open, car moving
options.why: This is the safety invariant: never move unless the doors are closed.

options.text: Doors closed, car moving
options.why: That's normal travel.

title: Weak safety rule
prompt: Tap the 2 words that make this safety rule useless.
sentence: The car should usually not move while the doors are open.
explain: Safety rules hold always: "The car must not move while any door is open."

title: Make it testable
prompt: Which lockout rule could a tester check?

options.text: Lock the account after too many wrong passwords.
options.why: How many is too many? For how long?

options.text: After 5 consecutive failed logins, lock the account for 15 minutes.
options.why: A count, what "consecutive" covers, and a duration.

options.text: Lock suspicious accounts as needed.
options.why: Who decides what's suspicious or needed?

title: Run the rule
prompt: Rule: "After 5 consecutive failed logins, lock the account. A successful login resets the count." A user fails 3 times, logs in, then fails 3 more. Locked?

options.text: Yes — 6 failures in total
options.why: The rule counts consecutive failures, and the success reset the count.

options.text: No — the count is 3
options.why: Running the rule step by step, like a model checker, shows the count is 3.

options.text: The rule doesn't say
options.why: This rule is precise enough to answer.
